title: Structure, Form & Theatrical Devices
description: The play's two-act structure, the play-within-a-play, Siobhan's narrator function, the graph-paper.
content_html:
Two Acts: The Play's Structural Spine

Simon Stephens's play is structured in two acts. Act 1 follows Christopher's investigation of Wellington's murder and his discovery of the hidden letters revealing that his mother is alive. Act 2 covers Ed's confession, Christopher's journey to London, his reunion with Judy, Roger Shears's hostility, his return to Swindon, the A-level exam, and the final scene with Siobhan. The two-act structure divides the play along a single dramatic axis: the revelation of the truth. Act 1 ends when the truth begins to emerge; Act 2 is the consequence of that truth.

This two-act structure is the primary formal difference between the play and Haddon's novel. The novel uses a prime-numbered chapter structure: chapters are numbered 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and so on through the sequence of prime numbers up to 233. This is a deliberately unusual formal device that communicates Christopher's mathematical mind on the page — the structure of the book is itself an expression of how Christopher thinks. This chapter system belongs to the novel only. In your Eduqas exam, never refer to chapters when writing about the Stephens play. The play has acts and scenes, not chapters.

Key Fact

The play has two acts. The prime-numbered chapter structure is a novel-only device — it does not exist in Stephens's play. In the exam, always refer to 'the play', 'the scene', 'Act 1', or 'Act 2', not to chapters.

The Play-Within-a-Play: Form as Meaning

The defining formal feature of Stephens's play is the play-within-a-play. Siobhan reads aloud from Christopher's book while Christopher acts out the events. This creates a double layer of performance: the audience watches Siobhan reading and Christopher enacting simultaneously. The gap between these two registers — written account and physical enactment — is where the play's most interesting meanings are made.

In Haddon's novel, this structure is described as a book-within-a-book: the novel you are reading is the book Christopher is writing. Stephens translates this into a play-within-a-play. The theatrical effect is different from the literary one: where the novel's metafiction creates a playful collapsing of reader and text, the play's structure creates a live relationship between narrator and character. Siobhan is not just reading — she is interpreting. Her compassionate, precise reading of Christopher's flat, logical prose reveals its emotional weight.

Translating Novel Devices into Theatre

Haddon's novel uses several formal devices that cannot be reproduced in performance. Understanding how Stephens translates them is essential for AO2 analysis of form and structure:

Prime-numbered chapters — novel only. Stephens replaces this structural expression of Christopher's mathematical mind with theatrical equivalents: the graph-paper set, mathematical projections on the walls, and the post-curtain maths scene.

Printed diagrams, maps, and mathematical proofs — novel only. In the play, Bunny Christie's set design and Finn Ross's video projections create the theatrical equivalent: mathematical sequences are projected on the graph-paper walls. The stage becomes a space that expresses Christopher's visual and mathematical thinking.

First-person prose narration — novel only. In the play, this is replaced by Siobhan's co-narration. The emotional intimacy of the novel's first person becomes the theatrical intimacy of Siobhan reading Christopher's words directly to the audience.

Director Marianne Elliott described the set as designed 'to be like Christopher's brain'. Designer Bunny Christie created a stage surrounded by graph-paper grid walls — the mathematical grid Christopher uses to understand spatial relationships. The set is not realistic: there are no rooms, walls, or furniture as such. Instead, the grid provides the underlying structure within which all the action occurs, and is activated by Finn Ross's video projections — mathematical sequences, the tube map, the lines of the train network — all rendered in the visual language of Christopher's thinking. The set communicates character: entering the play's space is entering Christopher's perception.

The Ensemble: Crowd, Voice, and Character

The play uses an ensemble cast. The same actors who play Christopher's neighbours and family members also function as voices, crowds, and environmental presences. This doubling is both practical (the play has many characters) and thematic: it represents Christopher's experience of a world in which individual identities blur into an overwhelming mass of stimulus.

The ensemble is most important in the train-station and Underground sequences in Act 2. Frantic Assembly's movement directors, Scott Graham and Steven Hoggett, choreographed these scenes to represent sensory overload: the cast physically surrounds Christopher, presses against him, moves at speeds and rhythms that threaten to engulf him. The theatrical effect is immersive — the audience experiences, however briefly, the sensory world that Christopher must navigate constantly. This is a theatrical device that prose cannot replicate.

Key Fact

The ensemble embodies the crowd in the train-station sequence. Frantic Assembly's choreography surrounds Christopher with physical movement, creating the experience of sensory overload for the audience as well as the character. This is a live theatrical effect — not describable, but experiential.

Christopher's Relationship with Metaphor

Christopher explicitly rejects metaphorical language. In Chapter 29 of Haddon's novel — communicated through Siobhan's narration in the play — Christopher explains that metaphors are lies: 'I think it should be called a lie because a pig is not like a day and people do not have skeletons in their cupboards.' He objects to the common idioms that neurotypical people use casually: expressions that are literally untrue but figuratively meaningful. Christopher's world is one of literal truth; metaphor is a form of untruth he cannot accept.

This is significant for AO2 analysis: Stephens's play operates against Christopher's preference. The graph-paper set is a metaphor for his mind. Siobhan's narration is a theatrical metaphor for first-person voice. The ensemble crowd is a metaphor for sensory overload. The play uses theatrical metaphor throughout to represent a character who distrusts metaphor — creating a productive tension between form and character.

Scenes Running Together: The Play's Temporal Structure

In the Stephens play, scenes run into one another without interruption, regardless of changes in location, time, or chronology. This fluid staging is another expression of Christopher's perspective: his account of events moves at the speed of his thinking rather than the conventional pace of realistic drama. There are no blackouts between scenes, no set changes that impose the standard theatrical grammar of 'and now we move to a different place'. The action flows continuously, just as Christopher's written account flows in his book.

In your exam response, always move from identifying a technique to explaining its effect on the audience and then connecting it to a wider theme. For example: state what the playwright does, explain how they do it using precise language, and argue what this reveals about character, theme, or context. This three-step approach — what, how, why — will take your analysis to the top band.

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.
exam_tip_html: Structure and form questions are where you can demonstrate the most sophisticated analysis. Show that you understand the distinction between the novel's devices (prime-numbered chapters, printed diagrams, first-person prose) and the play's devices (two-act structure, play-within-a-play, ensemble, projections, Siobhan's narration). For AO2, analyse how specific theatrical devices create meaning — not just what they are, but what they do.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play has two acts — never refer to chapters, which are a novel-only device.
  • Stephens translates the novel's prime-numbered chapters, printed diagrams, and first-person narration into theatrical equivalents: the graph-paper set, projections, and Siobhan's co-narration.
  • The ensemble cast embodies crowds and creates sensory overload in the train-station sequence — a theatrical effect that prose cannot achieve.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the structure of the play to create dramatic impact?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive structural analysis. Discusses: the two-act structure and its dramatic axis (revelation), the play-within-a-play as the overarching formal device, the fluid scene transitions representing Christopher's account, and the post-curtain maths scene as a structural epilogue. AO2: how structure creates meaning, not just organises events. Connects to themes: Act 1 as world before truth, Act 2 as world transformed by truth.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear structural analysis with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement with structure.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points about the play's organisation.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use theatrical devices to present Christopher's experience of the world?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of multiple theatrical devices. Discusses: the graph-paper set as Christopher's perceptual world, projections representing his visual-mathematical thinking, the ensemble as sensory overwhelm, Siobhan's narration giving his inner voice theatrical presence, the post-curtain maths scene celebrating his mode of understanding. AO2: each device must be analysed for what it does, not just described.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis of several devices with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Some awareness of theatrical form.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Stephens's adaptation translates Haddon's novel-specific devices into theatrical equivalents.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of specific translation choices: prime-numbered chapters → two-act structure + graph-paper set; printed diagrams → projections; first-person narration → Siobhan's co-narration; mathematical appendix → post-curtain maths scene. What is gained and what is lost in each translation? AO4: Stephens's adaptation challenge and choices.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis of some translation choices.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement with adaptation.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the ensemble cast and Frantic Assembly's movement to present Christopher's experience of the train station?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the staging. Discusses: ensemble as crowd, physical surroundment of Christopher, the choreographic language of sensory overload, and why this theatrical device creates an immersive experience the audience shares with Christopher. Compare to how a novel would present this (narration, description) and what is unique to performance. AO4: Frantic Assembly's contribution.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with theatrical awareness.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Christopher's rejection of metaphor create tension with the theatrical form of the play itself?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the productive tension between character and form. Christopher distrusts metaphor: 'a pig is not like a day.' Yet the play is built from theatrical metaphors — the graph-paper set (Christopher's mind), the ensemble (sensory overload), Siobhan's narration (his voice). Discusses what this tension means: is Stephens making a point about the impossibility of understanding Christopher without metaphor? AO2: form and content in tension.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis of the tension.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does the play-within-a-play structure create a 'double perspective' for the audience?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the double perspective: what Siobhan reads (Christopher's written account) vs what the audience sees Christopher do (physical enactment). The gap between these two creates interpretive space: Siobhan's compassionate narration reveals emotional depth that Christopher's literal presentation cannot. Connects to the novel's equivalent: the reader's double perspective on Christopher's first-person narration. AO2: the theatrical mechanism of the device.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

knowledge_checks.q: How many acts does the Stephens play have?
The prime-numbered chapter structure is a device found in:
options: Haddon's novel only — not in the Stephens play
Both the novel and the play
Neither — it was invented for this lesson

knowledge_checks.q: The graph-paper grid set was designed by _____, and was intended to represent Christopher's brain.
Christopher rejects metaphors because he believes they are lies — for example: 'a _____ is not like a day'.
Match each novel device to its theatrical equivalent in Stephens's play:
right: Two-act structure with graph-paper set and mathematical projections
Siobhan's co-narration reading from Christopher's book
Post-curtain maths scene staged with music, lights, and projections

flashcard_questions.q: How many acts does the Stephens play have, and why are chapters irrelevant?
flashcard_questions.a: Two acts. The prime-numbered chapter structure belongs to Haddon's novel only — the play uses scenes and acts. Never refer to chapters in the exam.
Siobhan reads from Christopher's book while Christopher acts out events. Two registers simultaneously: narration (Siobhan) and enactment (Christopher).

flashcard_questions.q: What theatrical equivalent does Stephens use for the novel's printed diagrams and mathematical proofs?
flashcard_questions.a: Finn Ross's video projections on the graph-paper walls — mathematical sequences visualised as part of the stage design.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Marianne Elliott describe the set as 'like Christopher's brain'?
flashcard_questions.a: The graph-paper grid designed by Bunny Christie reflects Christopher's mathematical and spatial thinking — the stage itself expresses his perceptual world.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the ensemble do in the train-station sequence?
flashcard_questions.a: They physically embody the crowd, surrounding Christopher and creating the sensory overload he experiences — choreographed by Frantic Assembly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the quote about Christopher's rejection of metaphor?
flashcard_questions.a: 'I think it should be called a lie because a pig is not like a day and people do not have skeletons in their cupboards.' He objects to.

flashcard_questions.q: What tension exists between Christopher's rejection of metaphor and the play's theatrical form?
flashcard_questions.a: Christopher distrusts metaphor, but the play uses theatrical metaphors throughout (graph-paper set, ensemble as crowd, Siobhan's narration). The play represents him through the very devices he rejects.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the play's fluid scene structure reflect Christopher's perspective?
flashcard_questions.a: Scenes run into each other without interruption, regardless of location or time — mirroring the continuous flow of Christopher's written account rather than conventional realistic drama.

glossary_terms.definition: A theatrical structure in which one story is performed within the frame of another — here, the performance of Christopher's book constitutes the play itself.
A group of performers who share roles and work collectively — in this play, the ensemble plays multiple characters and physically embodies crowds and environments.
A narrative technique that self-consciously draws attention to its own fictional status — in Haddon's novel, the book you read is the book Christopher is writing.
Video or image content displayed on the stage set — used in this production to render Christopher's mathematical thinking visually on the graph-paper walls.
A staging choice that represents something other than itself — the graph-paper set is a theatrical metaphor for Christopher's mind.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.
